analysis.one_liner: Required large meatpackers to report livestock prices and banned packer retaliation against ranchers.
analysis.headline: Twelve senators — 11 Democrats and 1 Republican — backed the bill, but it never got a hearing or a vote and died in the Senate Agriculture Committee when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required slaughterhouses handling more than 5% of a species' national slaughter to report prices and terms of sale to the Agriculture Department within 24 hours, with fines or up to five years in prison for refusing. It would have let the USDA ban anti-competitive buying practices, defined "captive supply" cattle, banned packers from retaliating against ranchers who speak out, and allowed triple damages for retaliation. It also required public import and export price data, a study of federal lending's role in livestock market concentration, a plan to consolidate food inspection, labels for U.S.-produced meat, and weekly public reporting of bulk cheese spot prices.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle, hog, and lamb producers, who sell to a handful of large packers. Price reporting would give them the same market information the packers hold; the retaliation ban and triple damages would protect producers who testify or complain about packer conduct; and the authority to regulate noncompetitive practices would give the USDA a tool against unfair buying. Dairy farmers would gain from public bulk cheese price data, which feeds into milk price formulas. Consumers would get more transparent beef price and import data, and a U.S.-origin label on meat.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every slaughterer handling more than 5% of a species' national slaughter to report prices and terms of sale to USDA within 24 hours, with violators facing fines or up to 5 years in prison, and the data published only in aggregate so sellers see real market prices.

Bans packers from retaliating against any livestock producer for statements about packer conduct, sets up a special three-member panel to hear complaints, uses a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard, and makes retaliating packers liable for up to three times the producer's damages.

Adds a new prohibition on packer practices that the Secretary of Agriculture, after consulting producers, determines are detrimental noncompetitive practices in livestock procurement or meat sales — a direct competition tool against concentrated buyers.

Defines 'captive supply' as livestock obligated to a packer more than 7 days before delivery, and requires near-real-time public reporting of import and export prices and quantities of meat and livestock, closing information gaps packers could exploit.

Orders weekly public reporting of statistically reliable bulk cheese spot-transaction prices from all cheese manufacturing areas, aiding dairy producers whose milk prices are tied to cheese markets, and speeds up the Fund for Rural America's funding dates.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking firms, which would bear the cost of 24-hour mandatory reporting, exposure to regulation of their buying practices, and up to treble-damages liability for retaliation. Slaughterers who knowingly refuse to report face fines or up to 5 years imprisonment. The U.S.-origin labeling system would be paid for with federal appropriations, and taxpayers would fund the interagency study and the food-inspection consolidation plan.

drawbacks.text: The anti-competitive practices provision gives the Secretary of Agriculture broad, open-ended power to declare any procurement practice 'detrimental noncompetitive' by regulation, without defining standards — creating regulatory uncertainty for the whole livestock trade.
The penalty for knowingly failing to report is criminal — up to 5 years imprisonment — a heavy sanction for a data-reporting requirement, even if limited to large slaughterers.

Large parts of the bill would not directly change conditions: it only orders a study of federal lending's role in livestock concentration and only requires the President to prepare a food-inspection consolidation plan, and price transparency alone would not force packers to pay more for cattle.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The enforceable core — mandatory price reporting, a retaliation ban with triple damages, and import/export data — would have shifted real bargaining power toward ranchers at a cost borne mostly by the packers who hold the information advantage. But the bill is more modest than its title suggests: its competition tool is a vague regulatory grant, and its concentration and food-safety provisions are studies and plans rather than action. On balance a genuinely useful bill for producers and consumers, with design weaknesses an honest supporter would concede.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in July 1996, and it sat there with no hearing or vote until the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the Cattle Industry Improvement Act of 1996 on July 11, 1996 and delivered introductory remarks on the floor.
The same day the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
Twelve senators signed on — 11 Democrats and 1 Republican, including Leahy, Harkin, Wellstone, Feingold, Dorgan, and Conrad.
The action history records nothing after the referral: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies, which kept price reporting voluntary, faced no new limits on their buying practices, and carried no retaliation liability. The ranchers and dairy farmers the bill aimed to protect gained nothing from it.

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.role: Senate Minority Leader; sponsor from South Dakota
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Richard Lugar
against.role: Chair, Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the bill was referred to his committee; it received no hearing or markup before the Congress ended.

against.name: Meatpacking industry
against.role: Industry groups opposing mandatory price reporting and packer regulation in this era
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed mandatory livestock price reporting and packer-conduct rules, which the bill's provisions would have imposed.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly all Democratic — 11 Democrats and 1 Republican among 12 signers — and because no vote was ever held, party positions beyond that are unknown.

industries.note: The bill strips packers of their private price information advantage, exposes their buying practices to regulation, and makes them liable for triple damages if they retaliate against producers. Packers' interest runs directly against the ranchers selling to them.

Producers would get the same real-time price and import/export data packers have, protection from retaliation when they speak out, and a USDA tool against unfair procurement practices. These are mostly small family operations, not a concentrated industry.

industries.industry: Bulk cheese spot-market traders and dairy processors
industries.note: Weekly public reporting of spot bulk cheese prices would end the opacity of thin trading arenas whose prices feed dairy price formulas — information asymmetry that has historically benefited market insiders.

The U.S.-origin labeling system would give domestic meat a distinct label, and public import price and quantity data would remove information advantages importers and their trading partners currently enjoy.
